\chapter{How Much and How Fast}
\label{ch:hi-how-much-and-how-fast}
\hlchaptermodality{64}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say how much and how fast in Hindi when I answer someone.}

Complete HI-C64-more and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ab]{\hi{अब} (ab) — now, from this point on}

\label{lesson:HI-C64-now}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{dard} mean, and what did \emph{bukhār} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{अब}}
\textbf{\hi{अब}} (\emph{ab}) — \textquotedblleft{}now, from this point on\textquotedblright{}.

The dictionaries do not agree on where \hi{अब} came from, and this book will say so rather than invent a chain. What it does is clear enough, and that is worth more here than a pedigree.

\hi{अब} draws a line: everything before it was one way, and from here on things are another. That is what separates it from \hi{अभी}, which you already own — \hi{अभी} is this very second, \hi{अब} is from this second onward. \emph{ab} and \emph{abhī} look alike and do different work.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words of degree and pace.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ab}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ab}, then \emph{abhī}, and say which one draws a line
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{अब} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}now, from this point on\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jaldī]{\hi{जल्दी} (jaldī) — quickly, soon}

\label{lesson:HI-C64-quickly}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ab} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{जल्दी}}
\textbf{\hi{जल्दी}} (\emph{jaldī}) — \textquotedblleft{}quickly, soon\textquotedblright{}.

From Persian \emph{jald}, 'brisk, quick', itself an Arabic word, with the ending Persian hangs on such words to make a quality-word. So \hi{जल्दी} began as 'quickness' and ended up doing the work of 'quickly' and 'soon' at once.

Hindi still keeps both jobs alive. \hi{जल्दी} on its own tells someone to hurry; \hi{जल्दी} beside a plan means it will happen before long. The word does not distinguish speed from nearness in time, and speakers hear which one from the sentence around it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{jaldī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{jaldī}, then \emph{phir milenge}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{जल्दी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}quickly, soon\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dhīre]{\hi{धीरे} (dhīre) — slowly}

\label{lesson:HI-C64-slowly}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{jaldī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{धीरे}}
\textbf{\hi{धीरे}} (\emph{dhīre}) — \textquotedblleft{}slowly\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{धीर} (\emph{dhīra}), which meant steady, calm, firm of mind. Hindi's word for slow is the old word for unhurried, and the compliment inside it never quite left.

Doubled — \hi{धीरे} \hi{धीरे} — it means 'little by little', and that doubled form is the one you will hear most. Saying a word twice to mean a gentle continuing is one of the most useful habits Hindi has.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dhīre}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dhīre}, then \emph{jaldī}, and say which one you would ask a speaker for
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{धीरे} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}slowly\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kam]{\hi{कम} (kam) — little, not much}

\label{lesson:HI-C64-little}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{dhīre} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{कम}}
\textbf{\hi{कम}} (\emph{kam}) — \textquotedblleft{}little, not much\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \emph{kam}, 'few, little', taken in whole. It answers 'how much' with a shrug downward, and it can sit in front of almost anything a speaker wants to play down.

One warning, and it is about our letters rather than about Hindi. \hi{कमरा}, the room you learnt in the house arc, begins with the same two sounds and has nothing whatever to do with \hi{कम} — it walked in from Portuguese. In Devanagari nobody would confuse them; in a romanization \emph{kam} and \emph{kamrā} sit uncomfortably close.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kam}, then \emph{kamrā}, and say which one is Persian
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{कम} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}little, not much\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zyādā]{\hi{ज़्यादा} (zyādā) — a lot, more}

\label{lesson:HI-C64-more}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{ज़्यादा}}
\textbf{\hi{ज़्यादा}} (\emph{zyādā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a lot, more\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \ar{زيادة} (\emph{ziyāda}), 'an increase', through Persian. It is the exact counterweight of \hi{कम}, and the two of them are the fastest way in Hindi to answer 'how much' without naming a number.

The nukta under the \hi{ज़} is doing real work, the same as in \hi{ज़रूर}. Drop it and you have a different consonant; keep it and you have the sound Persian and Arabic brought with the word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{अब}, \hi{जल्दी}, \hi{धीरे}, \hi{कम}, \hi{ज़्यादा}. Enough to answer how much and how fast.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{zyādā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{bilkul}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{ज़्यादा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a lot, more\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
